disease_desc: A disease is a condition that affects the normal structure or functioning of the body or mind. It may be caused by infections, genetic factors, problems with the immune system, environmental exposures, or changes in how the body works. Diseases can cause signs and symptoms such as pain, fever, tiredness, swelling, or changes in normal body functions, although some may have few noticeable symptoms. Some diseases are short-term, while others are long-lasting. Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment depend on the specific condition and may include healthy habits, vaccination, medicines, or other care recommended by a qualified healthcare professional. This is general educational information, not a diagnosis or a substitute for professional medical advice.

Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It most often affects the lungs, but it can affect other parts of the body. Possible symptoms include a cough lasting several weeks, chest pain, coughing up blood, fever, night sweats, tiredness, and unintended weight loss. TB can usually be cured with a complete course of specific antibiotics prescribed by a clinician; treatment must not be stopped early. Seek medical assessment if TB is suspected, and follow local advice to reduce spread.

A cough is a reflex that helps clear mucus, irritants, or germs from the airways. Common causes include viral respiratory infections, allergies, asthma, smoke or pollution exposure, acid reflux, and some medicines. A cough may be dry or produce mucus, and the cause cannot be determined from the symptom alone. Get medical advice for a cough that lasts more than a few weeks or is worsening. Seek urgent care for breathing difficulty, chest pain, coughing up blood, confusion, or severe illness.

Influenza (flu) is a contagious respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses. Symptoms often begin suddenly and may include fever or chills, cough, sore throat, runny or blocked nose, muscle aches, headache, and marked tiredness. Flu is different from the common cold, although symptoms can overlap. Rest and fluids may help with comfort; antiviral medicines may be appropriate for some people when prescribed promptly. Seek urgent medical care for breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion, dehydration, or symptoms that improve and then become worse.

Fever is a rise in body temperature, commonly related to an infection but sometimes caused by other conditions. It is a symptom rather than a disease, and the cause depends on the person's age, temperature, duration, and other symptoms. Drink fluids if safe for you, rest, and monitor symptoms. Seek medical advice for persistent or worsening fever. Urgent assessment is needed for difficulty breathing, confusion, stiff neck, seizure, severe dehydration, or other serious symptoms; infants and people with significant chronic illnesses may need earlier assessment.

Obesity is a chronic condition involving excess body fat that can increase the risk of health problems such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, sleep apnoea, and joint problems. In adults, body mass index (BMI) is one screening measure, but it does not assess health on its own and should be interpreted in context. Care may include sustainable eating habits, appropriate physical activity, sleep and behavioural support, and medical treatment when indicated. A healthcare professional can help create a safe, individualised plan without stigma.
